Let <MATH_0001> be a scheme, and let <MATH_0002> be an algebraic space over <MATH_0003>.
Let <MATH_0004> be a pre-relation over <MATH_0005>.
Let <MATH_0006> be a geometric point of <MATH_0007>.
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> We say <MATH_0008> are
<TEXTITOPEN_0001>weakly <MATH_0009>-equivalent<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if they are in the same equivalence class
for the equivalence relation generated by the relation
<MATH_0010>.
<STRUCT_0003> We say <MATH_0011> are
<TEXTITOPEN_0002><MATH_0012>-equivalent<TEXTITCLOSE_0002> if for some overfield <MATH_0013>
the images in <MATH_0014> are weakly <MATH_0015>-equivalent.
<STRUCT_0004> The <TEXTITOPEN_0003>weak orbit<TEXTITCLOSE_0003>, or more precisely the <TEXTITOPEN_0004>weak <MATH_0016>-orbit<TEXTITCLOSE_0004>
of <MATH_0017> is set of all
elements of <MATH_0018> which are weakly <MATH_0019>-equivalent to <MATH_0020>.
<STRUCT_0005> The <TEXTITOPEN_0005>orbit<TEXTITCLOSE_0005>, or more precisely the <TEXTITOPEN_0006><MATH_0021>-orbit<TEXTITCLOSE_0006>
of <MATH_0022> is set of all
elements of <MATH_0023> which are <MATH_0024>-equivalent to <MATH_0025>.
<STRUCT_0006>

<STRUCT_0001>
It turns out that in good cases orbits and weak orbits agree, see
Lemma <REF_0001>. The following lemma illustrates
the difference in the special case of a pre-equivalence relation.
